LOCKFILE LICENSE CHECK · RUNS IN YOUR BROWSER

Is anything in your node_modules GPL?

Paid scanners such as FOSSA and Snyk answer this inside a platform. This page does the core of it for free: paste your package-lock.json and get every dependency licence, with strong-copyleft, unlicensed, weak-copyleft and unknown packages listed first. SPDX OR/AND expressions are resolved.

Nothing is uploaded. The lockfile you paste is read in this browser and never leaves your device, and this tool makes no network calls of its own. It reads licence metadata that package authors declared; it is not legal advice.

Paste your lockfile

Paste a package-lock.json above and click Check licences.

Findings

PackageLicenceCategory

Want it as a CI gate?

Same logic, zero dependencies, one file plus the shared module. It reads one local file and nothing else:

node license-check.mjs                              # audit ./package-lock.json
node license-check.mjs --deny GPL-3.0-only,AGPL-3.0-only  # exit 1 if any appear
node license-check.mjs --fail-on copyleft --no-dev  # exit 1 on strong copyleft or unlicensed
node license-check.mjs --json                       # machine-readable

Get license-check.mjs and classify.mjs from the repo. Node 18+, nothing to install, no network calls.

Common questions

Which npm licenses are copyleft?

GPL, AGPL, SSPL and similar licences are strong copyleft: shipping code that includes them can oblige you to release your own source under the same terms. LGPL, MPL, EPL and CDDL are weak copyleft, which usually only reach modifications to the library itself. MIT, ISC, BSD and Apache-2.0 are permissive. The report lists every non-permissive package so a person can review it.

How does it handle OR and AND licence expressions?

For an OR expression such as (MIT OR GPL-3.0-only) the tool assumes you may choose, and scores the most permissive branch. For AND it scores the strictest. A WITH exception is scored as the base licence. Check the actual terms for anything you ship.

Does this tool upload my package-lock.json?

No. The lockfile is read in this page and never leaves your device. The page makes no network calls, and the CLI reads one local file.

Why do some packages show no licence?

npm only records a licence in the lockfile when the package declares one in its package.json. A package with none is reported as unknown, which is a prompt to read its repository, not a finding that it is unlicensed. Lockfile version 1 files record no licences at all.

Is this legal advice?

No. This is a heuristic read of licence metadata that package authors typed, which can be wrong or out of date. It is not legal advice and does not replace review by a qualified lawyer before you ship or sell software.

More: an npm licence compliance checklist for shipping software

Best-effort hosting, no SLA. These tools are free, experimental, and may be slow, broken, moved, or taken offline without notice. We do not promise uptime, backups of anything you type, or that a URL will keep working. Do not use this as a system of record. If a tool needs to survive, get license-check.mjs from the repo and run it yourself.

Everything runs in your browser. The lockfile you paste is never uploaded; there are no accounts, cookies, or analytics vendors, and the tool makes no network calls. Anonymous feature events (check_run, example_loaded) are counted only in local storage and can be deleted with the button below. Do Not Track and Global Privacy Control are honoured.

← Lockfile License Check

An npm licence compliance checklist for shipping software

A typical web app pulls in hundreds of packages, each with its own licence. Most are permissive. The few that are not are the ones worth ten minutes before a release, an acquisition review or a customer security questionnaire.

The categories this tool uses

  • permissive — MIT, ISC, BSD, Apache-2.0 and similar. Keep the notice; little else is required.
  • weak-copyleft — LGPL, MPL, EPL, CDDL. Changes to the library itself usually have to be shared; using it as a dependency usually does not.
  • strong-copyleft — GPL, AGPL, SSPL. Distributing (or, for AGPL and SSPL, offering over a network) software that includes it can carry obligations on your own code. Review these first.
  • unlicensed — UNLICENSED or SEE LICENSE IN .... No grant is visible in the metadata; read the file it points to.
  • unknown — no licence declared, or an identifier this tool does not recognise.

Checklist

  1. Run the check on package-lock.json, once with devDependencies and once with --no-dev: build tools you do not ship matter far less.
  2. Read every strong-copyleft entry's own repository. Declared metadata can be wrong.
  3. For a dual-licensed (MIT OR GPL-3.0) package, record which option you rely on.
  4. For an unknown package, look for a LICENSE file, then ask the maintainer to add a licence field.
  5. Add node license-check.mjs --fail-on copyleft to CI so a new dependency cannot add one silently.

What this does not tell you

It reads only the licence field package authors declared in their own package.json. It does not read licence files, detect code copied between packages, or follow transitive licences that npm did not record. It is a heuristic and is not legal advice.

No warranty. Provided free and as-is. It is not legal advice. Best-effort hosting, no SLA. The page makes no network calls and uploads nothing. Run the check.
